_README: THE BUILD PROTOCOL. This file IS a compile_commands.json -- a JSON
ARRAY of compile entries -- so any cc consumer reads it directly. Every
element before the last is a compile entry (the four standard fields
plus this protocol's extras, which a cc consumer ignores); the LAST
element is the NODE below, marked `protocol_version` (a compile entry
never has that key), carrying the sections a compile database cannot.
EXTRA ENTRIES ARE PERMITTED; THE ARRAY STRUCTURE IS NOT DISTURBED.
DESIGN RULE: everything is a RECORDING, replayed verbatim. The protocol
does not say 'these flags' and let a generator reassemble a command --
it records the command the build ran. Reassembling drifts, silently:
measured on a real project compiled with -fvisibility=hidden, letting
CMake rebuild the link lines produced -rdynamic and a LOCALISED main in
every executable, and 19 products differed while their code was
identical. So a unit, a product and a generated source each carry the
exact command that produces it, and the exact directory it runs in.
TWO SPELLINGS OF A PATH, load-bearing:
* under ${TREE} -- the replay MAKES it. It travels with the protocol.
This includes a WORKING DIRECTORY: the build tree is recreated, so
a command's cwd is spelled ${TREE}/... even though nothing
'produces' a directory.
* ABSOLUTE -- the replay only READS it (the project's own sources).
It does not move and must not be rewritten.
`$` is reserved: a literal dollar is `$$`; a bare `$` is refused.
A STEM MAY APPEAR TWICE, WHEN THE LANGUAGES DIFFER. A Fortran module and
the C it binds (`x.F90` + `x.c`) are two translation units with one stem;
a product's member (a stem) then resolves to BOTH objects. Two entries with
the same stem AND the same language is the error, not this.
The `directory` and `command` are the TOOLCHAIN's own -- nothing here is
CMake-specific. A make build records e.g. directory `${TREE}/source/mis`,
command `gfortran -g -std=legacy -c -o alg13.o alg13.f`. A make build whose
tree is IN SOURCE still spells its directory under `${TREE}`, so a replay
runs there rather than in the project it is proving.
_directory: The directory the command ran in. The command is replayed THERE, and any relative operand in it is relative to this.
_command: EXACTLY what the build ran, with every path under the tree re-rooted at ${TREE} and every path outside it left absolute. This is the authority -- a replay runs it, it does not re-derive flags from it.
_file: The unit's source. Under ${TREE} when the build GENERATED it; absolute when the project ships it.
_output: The object the command writes, as the build spelled it: RELATIVE to `directory` (the same convention cc uses). A replay reads the object's absolute path off this.
_stem: The unit's identity: ONE trailing extension removed, case kept. The protocol's key -- a product names its members as stems.
_language: The source's language, free-form ('c', 'cpp', 'fortran', ...). What a consumer needs to know to build the unit; NOT an identity.
_provides: Modules this unit DEFINES, as the SOURCE spells them (case kept). Omitted when empty.
_uses: Modules this unit USES, as spelled. Omitted when empty. Matching is case-insensitive where a consumer builds the graph.
_preprocess: The PREPROCESS command, when the build compiles the unit in TWO steps. A replay runs this first, then `command` (which consumes the intermediate this makes). Omitted when the build has no separate step.

_README: THE NODE. The last element of the array, marked `protocol_version`.
It carries everything a compile database cannot express. A cc-only
consumer skips it (it has no `file`/`command`).
A section with nothing to say is `[]` (or `{}`), never omitted: the
shape is the contract, and a section that appears only when a project
happens to use it makes two projects produce two shapes for the same
kind of fact.
_protocol_version: The only version this consumer reads. A file from another version is refused, not coerced.
comment: onboarded from <the directory this was captured from>
_capture: 'tree' is what ${TREE} means (the BUILD tree the replay recreates); 'layout' is 'in_source' or 'out_of_source'. Recorded, never re-derived -- a wrong guess re-roots every generated source.

products._kind: 'exe' | 'archive'. An 'archive' is a static library; set 'shared' for a .so/.dylib.
products._objects: For an 'exe': the STEMS of its own translation units.
products._members: For an 'archive': the STEMS that go into it.
products._libs: Libraries it links, in ORDER (ld resolves left to right). A library this protocol ALSO produces is linked by its output path; a foreign one keeps its path.
products._command: The EXACT link/archive command, replayed verbatim in `directory`. Nothing about the link line is re-derived (see the design rule).
products._directory: The directory the link ran in; its relative operands are relative to this.
products._shared: true when an 'archive' is a SHARED library (.so/.dylib). Load-bearing: linking a shared library leaves its symbols UNDEFINED in the consumer, linking a static one pulls them IN, so replaying a shared library as static changes every consumer's defined symbols.

_products: What the build LINKS. A replay runs each product's `command`; `objects`/`members`/`libs` say what it DEPENDS on, so the objects are built first.

generated_inputs._command: A SHELL LINE, replayed verbatim. It makes `output`.

_generated_inputs: Sources the build MAKES. A replay must reproduce them or it compiles a file that does not exist. Empty [] when the build generates nothing.
_own_roots: The tree-relative directories that are the project's OWN units, when its build pulls in third-party subprojects. Empty [] means every compiled unit is the project's.
_tests: The build system's OWN test registrations, as it reports them (ctest --show-only=json-v1). A replay re-registers them so the built tree is RUNNABLE the way the project runs it. Empty [] when none.
_support_files: Files a run READS that are neither compiled nor generated, carried as CONTENT. Empty [] when none.

_README: A PATCH op: a change the source needs to build on THIS platform/
toolchain, written so a fresh checkout reproduces it and a repeat pays
nothing. `check` is a SHELL line that exits 0 when the fix is ALREADY
there; `run` applies it. MEASURED on a real project: its Makefile
spelled target paths with backslashes (Windows) and its 1970s Fortran
used a dialect today's gfortran rejects -- both are prepare ops, so the
recorded protocol rebuilds from a clean checkout.

_prepare: Infrastructure the project needs ONCE (a submodule fetch, a patch, an overlay). Each carries a `check` so it runs AT MOST ONCE. Empty [] when none. Each op is IDEMPOTENT: it carries a `check` (a shell line, or a `{path, exists}` predicate) that exits 0 when it is already done. Ops that patch the source are how a project that needs a platform/toolchain fix stays reproducible.
_build: Toolchain-specific extras a CONSUMER may read (an optimization remap, module/include directories, policy flags). All OPTIONAL; {} for a project that declares none. NOTHING in this tool branches on them.
